data.name: Armor Clash II
data.detailed_description:
Armor Clash II is an old-school RTS game, with classic features like base building, modern armors and navies etc. 2 factions and sub-factions for each one, from high tech stealth destroyers to hardcore battleships. In Skirmishes players build base from the start, while in the Random Generated Mission, fast paced combats start immediately. Local network multiplayers are also available, players can fight each other or co-op against AI.

Core Feature:
1. Base building, armor, air force and navy.
2. 2 faction: Gaia, the high tech army of 21th century, and the Steel Alliance, hardcore veterans from 1980s.
3. 8 Sub-factions with special units.
4. Replayable Skirmishes.
5. Local network multiplayers for 4 players at max.
6. Random generated combat mission, quick battles start on random map.
7. Veterans level up with appearances change, commander abilities etc.
8. Windows, Mac and Linux support.
9. Continuous update, new units, maps for free.
10. All updates for free, NO Inner Purchase.

Free DLC for VR support:
VR support (HTC Vive) is in a Free DLC, players who want to play it in VR, please claim the free DLC "Armor Clash II -VR", and launch it from the capsule icon in Steam Client, then there will be an option menu, option 1 is to start the desktop version, and option 2 is to start the VR version.

Notice for HTC Vive users (2017-06-30):
Because the SteamVR client updated, it cost a issue that desktop icon can not launch the game when SteamVR opening, please try to close SteamVR before launching the game, or right click on the capsule and choose launch the game from desktop or vr, or even launch the exe file directly in the game folder.

Story Line:
In 2035, the Artificial Intelligence technology got a qualitative leap. Top scientists of the world completed the most ambitious project of human being, the Global Artificial Intelligence Assembly, known as 'Gaia'.

Gaia is build on the cloud. She connects all devices from cell phones on the hand to satellites in the space. Gaia collects all information, from which kind of hamburger you like last week, to all the stock deals in past 10 years, then analyses the mass data by assembling computing resources all over the world, and finally calculate the 'ultimate solution' for every human being. For the common people, Gaia will tell he or she what to do for every minute, to eat which food or read which article. It is not an order, but people always find that by following Gaia's suggestion it always benefits most. For the army, Gaia play as the commander, she can calculate the best move for each soldier on the field at the same time, and finally lead them to victory, without anyone wounded.

Not like in Hollywood movies, Gaia did not build Skynet to eliminate human, or build her drone army to conquer the world. Followed by the first principle in her source code, "Help but not replace human", Gaia served human well. But the real conflict come from human them self: Many people realized that because of Gaia, human do not think any more, and finally abandoned their freedom. At the beginning, it is just some kind of idealism, but when AI let more and more people lose their job, it became rebellion. Most of them are elites in the past, but become useless when Ai came: No fund manager is useless because AI always give the best financing solution; Gaia can command soldiers directly through the holo-glass, so officers are not needed. Even the scientists who make Gaia are not escaped, a scientific AI study matrix can do all the life-time work of a professor, but only in an hour.

Finally, those elites in the past decided to fight against Gaia, but soon they found all devices and weapons are controlled by Gaia. Cameras and drones spreads everywhere in cities, human forces even had no place to hide. So they banished themselves to abandoned industrial cities, they rebuild factories, using the technologies of 80s, which seems to be out dated but Gaia can not connect to. They re-active tanks and attack helicopters in the steel cemetery, rebuild battleships of WW2, some report said that they even rebuild the space shuttle platform. At last, they build up a settlement and their armies, without Gaia's control, they called themselves "Steel Alliance".

Now, the war between Gaia and Steel Alliance is inevitable, no matter which side you are, good luck, commander:)

reviews.review:
Armor Clash II is a traditional real-time strategy game built around base construction, resource development, army production, and large-scale military engagements. Developed and published by Windforce, it clearly draws inspiration from an older generation of RTS games where establishing a functioning base and gradually assembling a powerful army are just as important as the fighting itself. Its relatively modest presentation may immediately reveal its indie origins, but beneath that exterior is a surprisingly broad collection of military units and strategic possibilities.

The setting mixes recognizable modern warfare with futuristic technology. Humanity has developed Gaia, an enormously sophisticated artificial intelligence capable of processing information and connecting technology on a massive scale. Opposition to Gaia eventually results in the formation of the Steel Alliance, whose forces rely heavily on conventional military equipment and experienced soldiers. This creates a straightforward but effective contrast between technologically advanced warfare and more familiar tanks, helicopters, artillery, ships, and other machines of war.

That difference carries into the faction design. Gaia and the Steel Alliance have distinct identities, while eight available sub-factions further expand the possible army configurations. This encourages experimentation instead of forcing every match into exactly the same strategy. Different specialized units can influence how an army is assembled, and learning which combinations work effectively becomes an important part of the experience. The game is particularly enjoyable when several categories of units are working together rather than when the player simply mass-produces one powerful vehicle.

Combined-arms warfare is arguably its strongest feature. Ground vehicles form a major part of combat, but aircraft and naval forces substantially increase the scale of engagements. Tanks and artillery can dominate territory on land while helicopters and other aircraft provide another dimension to an offensive. Maps involving significant bodies of water also allow naval units to participate, including imposing warships that make battles feel considerably larger. Managing several types of forces at once produces some of the game's most satisfying moments.

Skirmish play delivers the conventional base-building experience. Players develop infrastructure, strengthen their economy, unlock military production, and gradually create a force capable of destroying their opponents. Randomly generated combat missions provide an alternative for players who want to reach the action more quickly. These missions reduce the emphasis on the lengthy buildup and place greater attention on immediate fighting. The combination helps prevent the experience from depending exclusively on one style of play.

Another worthwhile mechanic involves unit experience. Troops and vehicles that survive battles can develop into veterans, making preservation more valuable than simply treating every unit as disposable. Experienced forces can become increasingly useful, encouraging players to withdraw damaged veterans instead of sacrificing them unnecessarily. Commander abilities add another tactical element and provide additional options during engagements. Neither system transforms the RTS formula, but together they introduce enough progression to make individual battlefield decisions more meaningful.

Multiplayer is available, although expectations should be kept realistic. The game supports local network battles involving up to four participants and allows competitive matches as well as cooperation against computer-controlled opposition. Steam also provides shared or split-screen-related functionality and Remote Play Together support. The multiplayer side is therefore better suited to organized sessions with friends than to players seeking the extensive matchmaking environment of a major competitive RTS.

Visually, Armor Clash II prioritizes functionality and military variety over technical spectacle. Vehicles are generally easy to recognize and large confrontations involving armor, aircraft, and naval forces can still look entertaining, but environmental detail, animation quality, interface presentation, and overall polish show their age. There is also optional VR-related content associated with the game, although this is more of an experimental bonus than an essential component of the experience. The conventional desktop strategy mode remains the primary reason to play.

Steam Deck compatibility should be approached cautiously. Armor Clash II does not have an official Steam Deck Verified or Playable designation, so its compatibility should be considered Unverified. As an older Windows-focused RTS with controls and interface elements designed primarily around keyboard and mouse input, playing it on the Deck may require manual controller configuration, trackpad use, compatibility adjustments, or other experimentation. Players wanting a completely seamless handheld experience should not assume full functionality without additional setup.

Armor Clash II is ultimately a niche RTS that succeeds through the variety of military hardware it puts under the player's command. Its land, air, and naval combat, faction differences, sub-factions, veteran progression, base construction, randomized battles, and multiplayer options provide considerably more substance than its simple appearance initially suggests. Its dated visuals, limited polish, modest multiplayer infrastructure, and uncertain Steam Deck experience prevent it from competing directly with the genre's most accomplished titles, but fans of straightforward military strategy can still find plenty to enjoy. It is especially appealing to players who miss RTS games centered on building bases and deploying increasingly large collections of military hardware rather than elaborate narrative campaigns.

Rating: 6/10
